title: Best Index Funds 2026: 5 Compared on Cost and Coverage
description: VTI, FZROX, SWTSX, SCHB, SPY — compared head-to-head on expense ratio, tax efficiency, and long-term compounding. Find the right fund for your brokerage.
lede: Expense ratios have converged so close to zero that picking the wrong index fund now costs you almost nothing — and yet the differences in tax efficiency, portability, and trading mechanics still matter over decades. These five funds cover nearly the same market but serve different investors in meaningfully different ways. Here is what separates them after you strip away the marketing.
methodology: Funds evaluated on five criteria: expense ratio, fund size and liquidity, tax efficiency (ETF structure vs mutual fund), brokerage portability, and historical tracking error vs the target index.

sections.heading: What to look for in a total-market index fund
paragraphs: The fund landscape looks identical on the surface — near-zero fees, broad diversification, passive management. The differences live in structure, tax treatment, and where you can hold them.

subsections.heading: Expense ratio: every basis point compounds
paragraphs: At a 7% annual return, a 0.09% expense ratio versus 0.00% costs roughly $9,000 on a $100,000 investment over 30 years. That gap narrows the longer you hold, but it never closes. For long-term buy-and-hold investors, the cheapest fund wins by default — assuming equivalent coverage.

subsections.heading: ETF vs mutual fund structure
paragraphs: ETFs trade intraday and carry a structural tax advantage: they can shed low-cost-basis shares via in-kind redemptions, avoiding capital gains distributions. Mutual funds distribute gains to all shareholders regardless of whether you sold. Over decades in a taxable account, this structural difference can outweigh a small expense ratio advantage.

subsections.heading: Index coverage: total market vs S&P 500
paragraphs: Total market funds (VTI, FZROX, SWTSX, SCHB) hold roughly 3,500–4,000 US stocks including small- and mid-caps. S&P 500 funds (SPY) hold 503 large-caps. Historically the return difference is small — small-cap premium is real but inconsistent — but total market funds give you full US equity exposure without a size bet.

subsections.heading: Brokerage portability
paragraphs: ETFs (VTI, SCHB, SPY) transfer freely between brokerages via ACATS. Mutual funds (FZROX, SWTSX) are generally brokerage-specific: FZROX cannot be held outside Fidelity, SWTSX requires Schwab. If you ever change brokerages, you must sell mutual fund shares — a taxable event in non-retirement accounts.

subsections.heading: Liquidity and bid-ask spread
paragraphs: SPY is the most-traded ETF on the planet with daily volume exceeding $20 billion and spreads of one cent or less. VTI has $400M+ in daily volume with similarly tight spreads. SCHB trades around $100M daily — more than adequate for individual investors. Bid-ask spread matters only if you trade frequently; buy-and-hold investors can ignore it almost entirely.

sections.heading: How the five funds have performed
paragraphs: VTI, SWTSX, and SCHB have tracked the same CRSP US Total Market Index (or close equivalents) within a few basis points annually for over a decade. Their 10-year annualized returns through 2025 are within 0.05% of each other — effectively identical. FZROX has existed only since 2018 but has tracked its proprietary Fidelity US Total Investable Market Index with near-zero error.

SPY tracks the S&P 500, which has outperformed total market funds in 8 of the last 15 years due to large-cap dominance. Over full market cycles, the difference is negligible — the 2000s saw small-caps outperform significantly. Neither approach has a durable edge; your preference for simplicity or completeness matters more than picking the historically-superior index.

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: If you want the lowest possible cost and live inside Fidelity's ecosystem, FZROX's 0.00% ER is hard to argue against — just understand you cannot transfer the shares if you leave. VTI is the consensus choice for taxable accounts at any brokerage: ultra-low cost, maximum liquidity, and the ETF structure minimizes capital gains distributions. SCHB is the identical pick for Schwab users who prefer their native fund family.

SWTSX makes sense only inside a Schwab retirement account where portability is irrelevant. SPY belongs in options strategies, institutional portfolios, and short-term tactical trades — its 0.09% ER is a needless drag for long-term buy-and-hold investors who can buy VOO at 0.03% for the same S&P 500 exposure. Match the fund to your brokerage and your time horizon, then stop thinking about it.

faqs.q: Is FZROX really free? What's the catch?
faqs.a: FZROX has a 0.00% expense ratio — no hidden fees inside the fund. The catch: it can only be held at Fidelity. If you move to another brokerage, you must sell (a taxable event outside retirement accounts). It also uses Fidelity's proprietary index, not a widely-licensed one like CRSP or Russell.

faqs.q: VTI vs SCHB — which is better for a Schwab user?
faqs.a: For a Schwab account holder, SCHB is the natural choice: same 0.03% ER, tracks nearly the same index, auto-invests without currency conversion friction. VTI is marginally more liquid, but for a buy-and-hold investor the practical difference is zero.

faqs.q: Why does SPY have a higher expense ratio than VOO?
faqs.a: SPY was created in 1993 under a trust structure that makes it legally difficult to lower fees. State Street's VOO-equivalent (SPY) launched decades before Vanguard's VOO and built its brand among traders who value its liquidity and options market. Long-term investors should use VOO (0.03%) or IVV (0.03%) instead of SPY for S&P 500 exposure.

faqs.q: Can I hold VTI in a Roth IRA?
faqs.a: Yes — VTI can be held in any brokerage's Roth IRA, traditional IRA, 401(k) brokerage window, or taxable account. Its ETF structure is especially valuable in taxable accounts where capital gains distributions would otherwise create a tax drag.

faqs.q: Total market fund vs S&P 500 fund — which has better long-term returns?
faqs.a: Neither has a durable edge over full market cycles. The S&P 500 outperformed in the 2010s due to large-cap tech dominance; the total market outperformed in the 2000s when small-caps led. The difference in any given 10-year window is typically under 0.5% annualized. Pick total market if you want complete US coverage; pick S&P 500 if you prefer the well-known benchmark.

products.review: VTI holds 3,700+ US stocks at 0.03% ER and is the default recommendation for taxable brokerage accounts. Its ETF structure means Vanguard can flush unrealized gains in-kind, and the fund has issued zero capital gains distributions since 2000. Works at any brokerage, trades with spreads under $0.02.
pros: Holds at any brokerage — fully portable
cons: 0.03% ER vs FZROX's 0.00% — tiny but nonzero
Must buy in whole shares unless brokerage supports fractional ETF trading

products.review: FZROX is the cheapest index fund in existence at 0.00% — Fidelity absorbs all operating costs as a customer acquisition strategy. The fund tracks Fidelity's proprietary US Total Investable Market Index with near-zero tracking error since its 2018 launch. The only real downside is portability: you cannot transfer shares out of Fidelity without selling.
pros: 0.00% expense ratio — truly free to hold
Mutual fund structure allows automatic investing in exact dollar amounts
cons: Fidelity-only: selling required if you change brokerages
Proprietary index, not CRSP or Russell — minor methodology differences

products.review: SWTSX is Schwab's mutual fund equivalent to VTI — 0.03% ER, tracks CRSP US Total Market, and allows dollar-based automatic investing without fractional share math. Inside a Schwab IRA or 401(k), it is the cleanest way to run a total-market allocation. In a taxable account, SCHB's ETF structure is the better choice.
pros: Dollar-amount investing, no fractional share headaches
CRSP index — same benchmark as VTI
cons: Mutual fund: capital gains distributions possible (rare historically)
Schwab-only in practice — transferring requires liquidating

products.review: SCHB is Schwab's ETF answer to VTI: 0.03% ER, tracks the Dow Jones US Broad Stock Market Index (3,500+ holdings), and trades with tight spreads at around $100M daily volume. The ETF structure means capital gains distributions are rare. For Schwab account holders who want ETF mechanics, this is the natural home.
pros: ETF structure: capital gains distributions minimized
Transfers freely to any brokerage via ACATS
cons: Slightly less liquid than VTI ($100M vs $400M daily volume)
Dow Jones index vs CRSP — minor methodology difference

products.review: SPY is the world's oldest and most-traded ETF, with daily volume exceeding $20 billion and the tightest options market of any equity fund. For long-term investors it is overpriced at 0.09% when VOO and IVV offer the same S&P 500 exposure at 0.03%. SPY earns its place for active traders, options strategies, and institutional hedging — not buy-and-hold retirement accounts.
pros: $20B+ daily volume — deepest liquidity of any ETF
Unmatched options market depth for hedging
cons: 0.09% ER — three times VTI's cost for similar exposure
S&P 500 only: misses small- and mid-cap stocks
